lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.because: Otherwise, use the institution’s accurate status.

items.because: The education section does not explain the doctoral specialty.

items.says: Use an en dash rather than a hyphen in the date range.
items.because: Date ranges should be consistent.

items.says: Make sure the education and research-assistant dates accurately show any gap or transition.
items.because: The research-assistant period falls between the B.S. and Ph.D.

items.says: Give the bakery role less prominence or place it in Additional Experience for quant applications.
items.because: It appears before the quantitative internship and receives substantial attention.

items.says: Use “labor” rather than “labour.”
items.because: The résumé otherwise uses U.S. conventions.

items.says: Clarify whether the six people were direct reports, per-shift staffing, or the total team.
items.because: The scope of management responsibility is unclear.

items.says: Add the actual budget result if available.
items.because: Staying within budget shows responsibility but limited measurable impact.

items.says: Remove unnecessary operational detail if space is tight.
items.because: It is less relevant than the quantitative work.

items.says: Describe the 12%-to-7% change as a five-percentage-point reduction or give cost savings.
items.because: The result would be more precise or show its financial impact.

items.says: Clarify the period over which waste was measured.
items.because: The improvement could otherwise appear anecdotal.

items.says: Be able to explain how the stock-count and ordering actions caused the reduction.
Give the Northpeak internship greater visual prominence than the bakery role.
items.because: It is the most relevant experience.

items.says: Confirm that the firm and results can be disclosed.
items.because: They may be subject to confidentiality restrictions.

items.says: Clarify whether the Sharpe change was for the desk book, a simulated subportfolio, or the signal.
items.because: Claiming one intern signal changed a desk book’s Sharpe may sound overstated.

items.says: Make unmistakable that the performance came from a backtest, not live trading.
Verify that the out-of-sample data was genuinely untouched or walk-forward.
items.because: Repeated tuning against that period would undermine the description.

items.says: Consider whether 18 months adequately supports the performance claim.
items.because: The strategy is short-horizon.

items.says: Define the futures universe more precisely if confidentiality permits.
Explain how daily turnover was calculated.
items.because: Turnover conventions differ.

items.says: Specify what “90% of gross returns” is measured against.
items.because: It could mean the original signal’s gross return, gross P&L, or another metric.

items.says: Replace “by a third” with an exact percentage if available.
Distinguish estimated slippage from observed execution costs.
items.because: The wording could be read as realized savings.

items.says: Verify that the Diebold–Mariano test was appropriate for nested models.
items.because: Standard DM inference can be biased in that setting.

items.says: Clarify what was forecast and which loss function was tested.
Resolve the reference to 30 indices versus the earlier liquid-index-futures universe.
items.because: The universe descriptions differ.

items.says: Account for multiple testing if 30 separate tests were conducted.
Remove “standard” unless it identifies a specific methodology.
items.because: It adds little and may draw attention to the test-selection issue.

items.says: Fix the sentence structure.
items.because: The introductory participial phrase does not align cleanly with the main clause.

items.says: Lead with the feature store rather than the data joining.
Clarify whether there were 120 features total or 120 per venue.
Separate the data-engineering work from the reuse impact if necessary.
items.because: The sentence is difficult to scan.

items.says: Be prepared to explain how point-in-time joining prevented look-ahead leakage.
Multiplying daily Sharpe by 252 is the wrong annualization method.
items.because: Daily Sharpe is generally annualized using the square root of 252 under the relevant conditions.

items.says: The bullet highlights an incorrectly reported risk metric rather than an achievement.
items.because: A résumé should not highlight that mistake.

items.says: Recheck the other Sharpe figures after correcting the annualization.
Clarify how the documentation’s first-week onboarding effect is known.
Support any quantified adoption claim.
Shorten the list of documented items if space is needed.
Use consistent comma style in the list.
Clarify whether the research-assistant role was post-baccalaureate.
items.because: It occurred after the B.S. and before the Ph.D.

items.says: Check the dates and titles if this role continued into the Ph.D.
Clarify whether the 72-hour and five-hour runtimes were comparable wall-clock measurements.
items.because: The compute resources may have differed.

items.says: Mention parallelization if it drove the speedup and is relevant.
Remove the first-person wording.
items.because: The rest of the résumé does not use it.

items.says: Specify authorship status if the paper has other authors.
items.because: The paper is under review.

items.says: Verify that naming JASA complies with review and disclosure expectations.
Clarify whether the log-factor improvement holds under the prior bound’s assumptions.
Identify the estimator or problem class more specifically if space allows.
Reflect the teaching duties in the title or a separate entry.
items.because: The bullet mixes research-assistant and teaching-assistant responsibilities.

items.says: Clarify whether all 12 problem sets were written independently.
State the basis of the 4.8/5 rating if it came from a formal course evaluation.
Consider removing the teaching bullet for highly technical industry applications.
items.because: Stronger research material may be available.

items.says: Split or reduce the bullet.
items.because: It combines four unrelated responsibilities.

items.says: Make “which” refer unambiguously to the R package.
items.because: Grammatically, it may refer to the entire preceding list rather than the package downloaded 3,000 times.

items.says: Prioritize package development and adoption over routine service work.
Move or remove cluster maintenance, reading-group organization, and grading unless needed.
items.because: They may not fill a specific requirement.

items.says: Clarify the download source and measurement period if asked.
Explain any overlap with the dissertation or Northpeak work.
items.because: The project could look like the same work reported twice.

items.says: Use “Present” only if the project is still active.
Add a public repository, paper, or report link if available.
List other major libraries only if they add useful signal.
Remove or heavily consolidate the volatility project’s overlapping results.
items.because: Its three bullets describe closely related improvements from the same model.

items.says: Specify the evaluation design.
items.because: It should establish that the result is genuinely out of sample.

items.says: Clarify how the 7% result was aggregated.
items.because: It could be an average across indices, a pooled result, or something else.

items.says: Include uncertainty or significance only if properly assessed.
Avoid repeating nearly identical “30 equity indices” wording across bullets.
The claimed 33% forecast-error improvement is arithmetically wrong.
items.because: A decline from 0.20 to 0.15 is a 25% reduction relative to 0.20.

items.says: Name the forecast-error metric.
items.because: “Forecast error” is too vague.

items.says: Clarify what 0.20 and 0.15 represent and whether lower is better.
Explain whether the added realized-volatility features were absent from the earlier baseline.
items.because: HAR-RV itself uses realized-volatility terms, making the description conceptually confusing.

items.says: Separate the effects of added features and asymmetric loss if their contributions cannot both be attributed.
Remove the bullet if it largely duplicates the QLIKE result.
The 52%-to-58% change is six percentage points, not a 6% relative increase.
items.because: The relative increase would be about 11.5%.

items.says: Define how direction was measured.
State whether 58% differs statistically from chance or the baseline if assessed.
Remove the repeated model and universe description if already clear.
items.because: Those details appear in the preceding bullet.

items.says: Keep the hit-rate metric only if directional accuracy matters to target roles.
Give the competition’s actual name if permitted.
items.because: The generic description is less credible and hard to verify.

items.says: Include a public profile or competition link if available.
Use a more precise percentile if retaining the top-2% claim.
items.because: 41st of 2,900 is about the top 1.4%, making top 2% conservative.

items.says: Clarify whether 41st was the final private-leaderboard placement.
Drop either the rank and field size or the percentile if space is limited.
items.because: They are somewhat redundant.

items.says: Be ready to explain the individual contribution within the team of three.

items.says: Identify the leakage mechanism prevented by time-grouped folds.
Explain the 0.02 score gap.

items.says: Do not treat the smaller local-to-leaderboard gap as definitive proof leakage was removed.
Clarify whether permutation importance used leakage-safe validation.
Quantify any runtime or complexity improvement if there was one.
items.because: Otherwise, the outcome is mainly a reduced feature count.

items.says: Ensure the unchanged validation score was measured on untouched folds.
